analysis.one_liner: Bans toxic flame retardants from children's products and upholstered furniture.
analysis.headline: A bill to ban eleven toxic flame retardants from children's products and furniture was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in August 2015 with no cosponsors and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal to sell or import children's products and upholstered furniture containing more than a trace of eleven named chemical flame retardants, chemicals linked in scientific studies to cancer, hormone disruption, and developmental harm in children, and to elevated cancer rates among firefighters who breathe their smoke. It would also require the Consumer Product Safety Commission to appoint a scientific panel to study all flame retardants and add more chemicals to the ban if they are found dangerous. The bill never left the Senate committee it was assigned to.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, pregnant women, and firefighters. Young children are the most exposed group because they chew on products and absorb chemicals from household dust; firefighters face some of the highest cancer rates of any workers, in part from burning flame-retarded furniture. The bill also benefits manufacturers who already make flame-retardant-free products by leveling the field against competitors who keep using the chemicals.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to sell, manufacture for sale, distribute, or import children's products or upholstered furniture containing more than 1,000 parts per million of eleven specified flame retardants, including TDCPP, TCEP, and chlorinated tris compounds, taking effect one year after enactment.

Requires the Consumer Product Safety Commission to appoint a chronic hazard advisory panel to study the health effects of all chemical flame retardants in these products, including cancer, developmental toxicity, endocrine disruption, and effects on firefighters exposed to combustion byproducts, and to add further chemicals to the ban by rule if they may cause substantial injury or illness.
Lets states keep stronger protections than the federal ban, since a state law is not considered inconsistent if it affords greater protection.

analysis.who_pays: Flame retardant chemical manufacturers lose the market for these chemicals in children's products and furniture. Furniture and children's product makers bear the cost of reformulating products and certifying they are free of the banned chemicals, though the bill skips a duplicative third-party testing requirement for this rule.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers would bear reformulation and certification costs on a one-year timeline, and some upholstered furniture and children's product makers argued such bans raise production costs without a proven fire-safety downside to removal, since flame retardants were added to meet fire standards.

Banning eleven named chemicals could push manufacturers toward substitute flame retardants not on the list whose safety is not yet established; the bill responds by ordering a study of the full range of retardants and letting the Commission add more to the ban, but that process would take years.

The bill exempts its own rulemaking from some procedural requirements of the Consumer Product Safety Act, speeding the ban but shortening the usual notice-and-comment process that lets affected parties object.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong: several of the named chemicals are known or suspected carcinogens and endocrine disruptors, children are exposed through household dust, and firefighters are exposed through smoke. The costs are real but ordinary for a product-safety rule — reformulation by furniture and toy makers, most of whom had alternatives available. The main weakness is the gap between the immediate ban and the slower process for restricting replacement chemicals.

outcome.mechanism: Schumer introduced it in August 2015, it was read twice and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, and it sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Charles Schumer introduced the Children and Firefighters Protection Act of 2015 in the Senate on August 5, 2015.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action — no hearing, committee vote, or floor vote — was ever recorded, and the bill died in committee when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies selling products with these flame retardants avoided a federal ban; no rule limiting the chemicals was adopted through this bill in that Congress.

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate; it received no cosponsors and no committee action.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Flame retardant chemical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: The flame retardant industry had a well-documented record of opposing bans on its products in states and at the federal level during this period.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill attracted no cosponsors, so the record shows no measurable support or opposition from either party.

industries.note: The bill would ban eleven of the industry's chemicals from two major consumer markets and give the CPSC power to add more. The industry profits from fire-safety standards that require its products, so removing that requirement removes its revenue.

industries.industry: Upholstered furniture and children's product manufacturers
industries.note: They would face reformulation and compliance costs within a year, but the bill waives the usual third-party testing requirement for this rule, and many manufacturers had already moved away from these chemicals.
Firefighters are exposed to combustion byproducts of these retardants and face elevated cancer rates; the bill requires the hazard panel to study exposures specific to firefighters.
